stem: Which quotation from a work by a seismologist would best support Ortega's claim?
stimulus: Slow slip events are episodes in which a section of fault creeps for days or weeks without producing noticeable shaking. They have often been described as a safety valve that bleeds off stress that might otherwise be released in a damaging earthquake. After analyzing a decade of GPS records from the Tavora subduction zone, seismologist Lucía Ortega contends that the valve metaphor is misleading, because slow slip can shift stress onto neighboring sections of the fault that remain locked.
choices: "Slow slip episodes at Tavora recurred roughly every fourteen months, a regularity that let researchers place instruments along the fault before each one began."
"After each slow slip episode, small earthquakes grew more frequent along the adjacent locked section, and borehole instruments there recorded a clear rise in strain."
"Within the creeping section itself, strain dropped sharply after each slow slip episode, falling to levels lower than any measured between episodes."
"Strain on the locked sections next to the creeping zone stayed essentially unchanged during each slow slip episode and in the months that followed."
explanation: Ortega's claim is specifically about where the stress goes: slow slip moves stress onto neighboring locked sections. Choice B reports rising strain and more small earthquakes in exactly that place, the adjacent locked section, right after each episode. That is the transfer the claim describes.

A.why: You picked a true-sounding detail about slow slip, its regular timing, that says nothing about stress moving to other parts of the fault.

C.why: This is the trap. The quotation is about the right subject, but it shows stress being released on the section that slipped, which is the 'safety valve' view. It says nothing about the neighboring locked sections the claim is about.

D.why: Unchanged strain on the adjacent locked sections would count against Ortega's claim. You matched the location the claim names but missed that the direction is reversed.

subtype_name: Which quotation from a scholar, survey or article supports the claim
license: CC BY 4.0 - original item, not College Board content
rated_why: Match specific claim to evidence while distinguishing from trap answer about same subject

stem: Which quotation from a work by an astronomer would best support Asante's conclusion?
stimulus: Meteor showers occur when Earth passes through trails of debris shed by comets. Because fresh trails are denser, astronomers have generally expected the most intense showers to come from debris released most recently. After reviewing records of forty meteor outbursts, astronomer Kwame Asante concludes that a trail's age matters less than whether Jupiter's gravity has compressed it into a narrow band that Earth then crosses.
choices: "Trails released within the last few decades were consistently denser than older trails, holding several times as many particles in each cubic kilometer."
"Jupiter's gravity can also nudge whole debris trails out of Earth's path, which explains why several confidently predicted showers never appeared."
"The most intense outbursts in the historical record all came from debris that the parent comets had shed within the preceding fifty years."
"Several of the strongest outbursts came from centuries-old trails that Jupiter had squeezed into tight ribbons, while younger, uncompressed trails produced modest displays."
explanation: Asante's conclusion has two parts: age matters less, and compression by Jupiter matters more. Choice D shows both. Old but compressed trails produced strong outbursts, while younger trails that weren't compressed produced weak ones.

A.why: This is the trap. It is about debris trails and their age, but it only shows that young trails are denser. That was the old premise. It says nothing about which trails produce the most intense showers or about compression by Jupiter.

B.why: You matched the mention of Jupiter's gravity, but this describes a different effect, moving trails out of Earth's path. It doesn't show that compressed trails give stronger showers.

C.why: If the strongest outbursts all came from recent debris, trail age would matter most. That is the view Asante rejects.

subtype_name: Which quotation from a scholar, survey or article supports the claim

rated_why: Identify that compression matters more than age, eliminating answers supporting opposite view

stem: Which quotation from a work by a folklorist would best support Vasko's claim?
stimulus: Versions of the tale of the clever miller, who outwits a greedy landlord by hiding grain in a dry well, have been recorded from the Baltic coast to the shores of the Caspian Sea. Some folklorists attribute the tale's wide range to independent invention, reasoning that grievances against landlords arose everywhere. Folklorist Irena Vasko disagrees, arguing that the tale traveled with merchants along river trade routes.
choices: "Variants collected in towns along the Volga and Dnieper share an odd detail, the miller's pet crow, that is missing from versions recorded just a few days' travel from those rivers."
"In nearly every recorded version, the landlord's greed is punished in a way that mirrors his own offense, a pattern that listeners across the region clearly relished."
"Tales of peasants outwitting their landlords appear in collections from regions with no known contact with one another, from rural Portugal to Korea."
"The earliest written version of the tale, preserved in a monastery chronicle, dates to the fourteenth century, although its oral origins are probably older."
explanation: Vasko's claim is about how the tale spread: along river trade routes. Choice A shows an unusual detail clustered in towns along the rivers and missing a short distance away. That pattern points to transmission along the rivers, not independent invention.

B.why: This is the trap. It describes a feature shared by almost all versions of the right tale, but a feature found everywhere says nothing about river routes. It fits the independent-invention view just as well.

C.why: Similar tales in regions with no contact are evidence for independent invention, the position Vasko argues against.

D.why: You were drawn to a fact about the tale's history. The date of its earliest written version doesn't show how or where it spread.

rated_why: Match transmission claim to geographic pattern evidence requiring inference about trade route spread

stem: Which quotation from a work by a hydrologist would best support Whitcomb's claim?
stimulus: In many mountain watersheds, beavers build dams that slow streams and spread water across floodplains. Water held behind these dams seeps into the surrounding soil, where it is stored and then gradually returns to the channel. Drawing on this process, hydrologist Dana Whitcomb claims that in drought years, beaver dams keep water flowing downstream later into the summer than it otherwise would.
choices: "Groundwater beside beaver ponds stood noticeably higher each spring than groundwater beside comparable undammed streams in the same watershed."
"In drought years, streams below beaver complexes ran dry earlier than streams without dams, because the ponds lost much of their water to evaporation."
"During the dry summer of 2021, reaches below beaver complexes kept flowing into September, while comparable reaches without dams went dry by late July."
"Beaver populations in the region have rebounded since trapping limits were introduced, and active dams are now found on most of its tributaries."
explanation: The claim has narrow scope. It is about drought years, flow downstream, and how late in summer that flow lasts. Choice C compares dammed and undammed reaches in a dry summer and shows the dammed ones flowing about six weeks longer. That is exactly the outcome the claim predicts.

A.why: This is the trap. It confirms only the middle link, water stored in the soil, and only in spring. It doesn't show that downstream flow actually lasts longer in late summer during a drought, which is what the claim is about.

B.why: This reports the opposite result: dammed streams drying up earlier in drought years. It would undercut Whitcomb's claim, not support it.

D.why: You picked a fact about how many beaver dams there are. It says nothing about how dams affect late-summer flow in drought years.

subtype_name: Which quotation from a scholar, survey or article supports the claim

rated_why: match specific drought-year claim to supporting evidence

stem: Which quotation from a work by an agronomist would best support Nandakumar's claim?
stimulus: Farmers who plant cereal rye in autumn and cut it down before sowing soybeans often find fewer weeds in their fields. Rye residue releases compounds that can suppress seed germination, and it also forms a mat that blocks light from reaching the soil surface. Agronomist Priya Nandakumar claims that the mat's shading, rather than its chemistry, accounts for most of this weed suppression.
choices: "Plots covered with rye residue had roughly 70 percent fewer weeds than bare plots, and the difference between the two held steady through midsummer."
"In plots where rye residue was rinsed repeatedly to strip out its suppressive compounds, weeds stayed nearly as sparse as under untreated residue."
"When rye residue was ground into powder and mixed into bare soil, weed germination fell almost as much as it did beneath an intact mat."
"Soybean yields in rye-covered plots matched those in plots treated with herbicide, which makes the cover crop an economical choice for many farms."
explanation: The claim compares two possible causes. It says shading does most of the work, not chemistry. Choice B removes the chemistry and keeps the mat, and suppression barely changes. That isolates shading as the main cause.

A.why: This is the trap. It confirms that rye residue suppresses weeds, but the claim is about which cause is responsible. This comparison with bare plots can't tell shading apart from chemistry.

C.why: Powdered residue gives no shade, so strong suppression here would point to chemistry. That goes against Nandakumar's claim.

D.why: You matched the topic of rye cover crops, but crop yield and cost say nothing about why weeds are suppressed.

subtype_name: Which quotation from a scholar, survey or article supports the claim
license: CC BY 4.0 - original item, not College Board content
rated_why: isolate shading effect by understanding what rinsing controls

stem: Which quotation from a work by a meteorologist would best support Reyes's conclusion?
stimulus: Cities absorb and radiate more heat than the surrounding countryside, and this warmth can push air upward, a key ingredient in thunderstorm formation. Meteorologists have therefore long asked whether urban heat makes storms stronger. After examining radar data from six inland cities, meteorologist Tomás Reyes concludes that the effect is real but displaced: the added rainfall is heaviest not over city centers but 20 to 50 kilometers downwind.
choices: "Across all six cities, summer storms dropped more rain within city limits than over rural land upwind, where storm totals were the lowest recorded."
"Urban heat is now the single largest influence on rainfall patterns in every inland region of the continent, outweighing both terrain and season."
"Downtown surface temperatures averaged 3°C above those of nearby farmland on summer afternoons, and the gap widened after sunset."
"Summer storm totals peaked in a band of suburbs and farmland lying downwind of each city, where they clearly exceeded the totals recorded downtown."
explanation: The key qualifier is where the extra rain falls: downwind of the city, not over its center. Choice D places the rainfall peak downwind and shows it beating downtown totals. That is the displacement Reyes describes.

A.why: This is the trap. It shows that cities get more rain than rural land upwind, so it supports an urban effect in general. It says nothing about the downwind zone, which is the specific point of the conclusion.

B.why: This makes a sweeping claim about every inland region that goes far beyond six cities. It also never says where the added rain falls.

C.why: This confirms that cities are hotter, which is the background premise. It says nothing about rainfall or where it falls.

subtype_name: Which quotation from a scholar, survey or article supports the claim

rated_why: recognize that displacement is the specific element of the claim

stem: Which quotation from a work by a music critic would best support Aas's claim?
stimulus: The late string quartets of the composer Halvard Lunde have long puzzled listeners with their abrupt, lopsided rhythms. Because Lunde grew up in a valley known for its fiddle music, critics have often heard echoes of that tradition in the quartets' melodies. Musicologist Signe Aas argues that the debt runs through rhythm instead: Lunde borrowed the fiddlers' uneven dance meters while writing melodies entirely his own.
choices: "Lunde's letters show that he listened eagerly to the valley's fiddlers as a boy and later called their music the foundation of everything he wrote."
"Lunde's melodies share the ornamented, drone-backed character of the valley's fiddle tunes, and several phrases echo tunes collected from local players."
"The quartets' irregular pulse closely matches the valley's springar dance, with its unequal beats, yet no tune in them corresponds to any collected fiddle melody."
"Audiences at the quartets' premieres were sharply divided, with some critics praising their boldness and others dismissing them as incoherent."
explanation: Aas's claim has two sides: the rhythm is borrowed and the melodies are not. Choice C shows both. The quartets' uneven pulse matches the local dance, and none of their tunes matches a collected fiddle melody.

A.why: This is the trap. It strongly shows that fiddle music influenced Lunde, but only in general. It doesn't show that the influence came through rhythm rather than melody, which is the point of Aas's claim.

B.why: Melodies that echo local fiddle tunes support the older melody view and conflict with Aas's point that the melodies were entirely Lunde's own.

D.why: You picked a detail about how audiences received the quartets. It says nothing about where their rhythms or melodies came from.

rated_why: distinguish rhythm-borrowed from melody-original in answer choice

stem: Which quotation from a survey respondent would best support Imbert's conclusion?
stimulus: After the city converted two car lanes on Carver Avenue into bus-only lanes, planners surveyed riders about the change. Average trip times had fallen only slightly, by about two minutes. Even so, most riders rated the new lanes highly. Planner Rosa Imbert concluded that riders valued the change mainly because it made their arrival times predictable, not because it made their trips faster.
choices: "My ride isn't much shorter, but now it takes twenty-five minutes every single day, so I've stopped leaving extra early just in case."
"I love the new lanes, because the bus flies right past all the traffic and I get downtown so much faster than I used to."
"The buses still get packed at rush hour, and I usually have to stand the whole way, which the new lanes haven't changed at all."
"The lanes work so well that the city should convert every major avenue in town to bus-only lanes as soon as it possibly can."
explanation: Imbert's conclusion is about why riders value the lanes: predictability, not speed. Choice A gives exactly that reason. The rider says the trip isn't much shorter but is now consistent, and that has changed how they plan.

B.why: This is the trap. The rider praises the lanes enthusiastically, but for speed, the very reason Imbert sets aside. It gives the right subject with the wrong reason.

C.why: Crowding is a real concern for riders, but this quotation says nothing about why riders value the lanes.

D.why: This jumps to a citywide policy recommendation and never says what the rider values about the lanes, so it can't show that predictability is the reason.

stem: Which quotation from a critic's review of a 1971 exhibition of Varga's work would most effectively illustrate Haddad's claim?
stimulus: In most print editions, every impression is meant to look the same, and small variations between sheets are treated as flaws. Printmaker Ilse Varga took the opposite approach in her late woodcuts. Instead of inking the carved block identically each time, she brushed on a different combination of colors before printing every sheet. Art historian Noor Haddad claims that this practice led viewers to focus on the differences among impressions of the same image rather than on any one sheet alone.
choices: "Varga's Harbor at Dusk is a masterful sheet, its deep ochre sky seeming to glow from within the grain of the wood itself."
"Set beside her early etchings, Varga's late woodcuts show how far she moved from fine, careful line toward broad, saturated color."
"Hung side by side, the twelve sheets of Harbor at Dusk kept visitors stepping back and forth, tracing how ochre or gray changed the scene."
"Varga's habit of inking each sheet differently was soon taken up by nearly every woodcut artist working in the city at that time."
explanation: Haddad's claim has a specific relationship in it: viewers compared different impressions of the same image instead of looking at one sheet by itself. Choice C shows exactly that. Visitors move between twelve sheets of one image and notice how the color changes alter the scene.

A.why: You picked a vivid quotation about the right print, but it praises a single sheet. Haddad's claim is that viewers looked past individual sheets to the differences among them, so this is on topic but doesn't support the claim.

B.why: This quotation does make a comparison, but between Varga's early and late periods, not between impressions of one image. You matched the idea of difference and missed what was being compared.

D.why: This quotation is about Varga's influence on other artists, which the claim never mentions. It also says nothing about how viewers looked at the prints, so it can't show the effect Haddad describes.

stem: Which quotation from an excavation report on Senna Hollow would most effectively support Arreola's claim?
stimulus: Obsidian is a volcanic glass that ancient peoples prized for making sharp tools. Each volcanic source leaves its own chemical signature, so archaeologists can trace where a piece of obsidian came from. Blades found at Senna Hollow, an inland farming village, have been traced to a volcano near the coast, roughly 200 kilometers away. Archaeologist Tomás Arreola claims that the villagers got this obsidian through exchange with coastal communities rather than by traveling to the volcano themselves.
choices: "Chemically, the obsidian at Senna Hollow matches the coastal volcano more closely than it matches any other known source in the region."
"The obsidian reached Senna Hollow as finished blades in a coastal flaking style, and no raw cores or quarrying waste turn up in the village."
"Residents of Senna Hollow clearly valued obsidian highly, often burying their most finely made blades alongside members of the household."
"Every household at Senna Hollow seems to have sent members on regular trips to the coast, where the volcano's slopes were easy to quarry."
explanation: The passage already establishes where the obsidian came from. Arreola's claim is about how it reached the village: through trade with coastal groups, not through the villagers' own trips. Choice B supports that. The blades arrived already finished in a coastal style, and the village has none of the raw material or waste that quarrying and toolmaking on site would leave behind.

A.why: This quotation confirms where the obsidian came from, which the passage already treats as settled. It doesn't separate trade from direct trips, and that is the specific point Arreola is making. It's on topic but doesn't support the claim.

C.why: You picked a detail about how the villagers used obsidian. How much they valued it tells you nothing about whether they traded for it or collected it themselves.

D.why: This quotation describes villagers traveling to the volcano and quarrying it themselves. That is the alternative Arreola rejects, so it works against the claim instead of supporting it.

stem: Which quotation from a researcher's report would best support Vance's argument?
stimulus: Along subduction zones, where one tectonic plate sinks beneath another, some fault segments creep in "slow-slip events" that last days or weeks and produce no shaking people can feel. Other segments stay locked and store strain until it breaks free in a major earthquake. Because slow slip moves one section of a fault, it can shift stress onto a neighboring locked section. Seismologist Teodora Vance argues that slow-slip events raise earthquake risk only indirectly: they matter when they load an adjacent locked segment, not because the slipping itself is dangerous.
choices: Slow-slip events preceded several of the largest subduction-zone earthquakes recorded over the past three decades, often by only a few weeks.
Large earthquakes followed slow slip only where a neighboring locked segment showed rising stress; elsewhere, slow slip passed without incident.
Slow slip usually relieves strain on the surrounding fault, leaving adjacent locked segments less likely to rupture in the following months.
Slow-slip events shook nearby towns hard enough to crack foundations, even in places where no larger earthquake ever followed.
explanation: Vance's claim has a qualifier: slow slip matters *only indirectly*, by loading an adjacent locked segment. To support it, a quotation has to show that the outcome depends on that middle link. Choice B does this. Earthquakes followed slow slip where a nearby locked segment was gaining stress, and they did not follow it anywhere else. That is the exact conditional relationship Vance describes.

A.why: You picked a quotation that links slow slip to big earthquakes, so it's on topic. But it never mentions a locked segment or stress transfer. It can't show that the link is indirect, and that's the specific point Vance makes.

C.why: You chose a quotation about slow slip and neighboring segments. It says slow slip makes those segments *less* likely to rupture, which is the opposite of Vance's claim that slow slip loads them with stress.

D.why: The passage says slow slip produces no shaking people can feel, and Vance argues the slipping itself isn't the danger. A quotation about slow slip directly damaging buildings goes against both points.

stem: Which quotation from Castellanos's study would best support the conclusion?
stimulus: Many plants in modern rainforests have leaves that end in narrow "drip tips," which channel rainwater off the leaf surface and may discourage the growth of fungi. Paleobotanist Imre Castellanos has examined fossil leaves from sediments laid down during a period when one region's climate grew steadily wetter. Castellanos concludes that drip tips arose independently in several unrelated plant families in response to the increased rainfall, rather than spreading outward from a single ancestral group.
choices: In the laurel family, leaves with drip tips become steadily more common in the layers deposited as the region's rainfall increased.
Modern rainforest leaves with drip tips dry more quickly after storms and carry fewer fungal spores than leaves without them.
Leaves with drip tips occur in three unrelated families in the oldest, driest layers and persist unchanged through the wetter ones.
Drip tips appear in three unrelated families only in layers deposited after rainfall increased, and none of their shared ancestors had them.
explanation: The conclusion has three parts: drip tips appeared in *several unrelated* families, they appeared *independently* rather than from one ancestor, and they appeared *in response to* wetter conditions. Choice D supports all three. It names three unrelated families, places the trait only after rainfall increased, and rules out a shared ancestor.

A.why: You matched the subject and the timing, but this quotation covers only one family. The claim is about several unrelated families evolving the trait independently, and a single lineage can't show that.

B.why: You picked a quotation about what drip tips do in modern plants. It repeats background from the passage and says nothing about when or in which fossil families the trait appeared.

C.why: This quotation has the right families, but it puts drip tips in the oldest, driest layers. If the trait existed before the climate got wetter, it can't have arisen in response to the extra rain.

stem: Which quotation from Felder's study would best support her claim?
stimulus: When cities replace curbside parking with protected bike lanes, shop owners often object that customers who arrive by car will go elsewhere. Yet cyclists and pedestrians tend to stop at shops more often than drivers do, which could make up for the lost parking. Urban planner Nadia Felder compared commercial streets in one city before and after such conversions. She claims that the conversions increase retail spending, but only on streets that already had heavy foot traffic; on quieter streets, she argues, the change makes little difference.
choices: Sales rose after conversion on streets with heavy foot traffic, while sales on quiet converted streets stayed close to earlier levels.
Across the city's converted streets, merchants reported higher average monthly sales in the year after the bike lanes opened.
Sales on busy streets fell after conversion, while quiet streets, which had few parked cars to begin with, saw no change.
Cyclists visiting converted streets made more frequent trips than drivers did, though they spent somewhat less on each visit.
explanation: Felder's claim depends on its scope words: spending rises *only* on streets with heavy foot traffic and makes little difference on quiet streets. Supporting it takes a comparison between the two kinds of street. Choice A gives that comparison: sales went up on busy streets and stayed about the same on quiet ones.

B.why: You saw that sales went up after the conversions and stopped there. This quotation averages all the converted streets together, so it can't show the busy-versus-quiet difference that Felder's claim depends on.

C.why: You noticed that this quotation splits busy streets from quiet ones. But it says sales on busy streets fell, which reverses the direction Felder claims.

D.why: This quotation is about how cyclists shop, which is part of the passage's background. It says nothing about how results differed by street type.

stem: Which quotation from a linguist's study would best support Osei's argument?
stimulus: Linguists have long observed that languages spoken across wide trading networks often have simpler grammars than languages spoken in isolated communities. One explanation centers on who learns the language. Children master even intricate grammatical endings with ease, but adults learning a second language tend to drop them, and if adult learners become numerous, their simplified usage can become the norm. Linguist Farida Osei argues that it is this influx of adult learners, not contact between languages in itself, that simplifies grammar.
choices: Languages carried along major trade routes generally show fewer grammatical endings than related languages spoken in remote valleys.
Children raised in trading towns learned two or three languages at once and mastered each one's grammar fully by age six.
Trade languages with few adult learners kept their complex endings, while those adopted by many adult learners steadily lost them.
Languages that many adults adopted as a second tongue gained new grammatical endings, even as their vocabularies shrank.
explanation: Osei separates two possible causes. She credits the adult learners and rejects "contact between languages in itself." A supporting quotation has to keep contact the same and let the number of adult learners vary. Choice C does this. All of the languages were trade languages, so all had contact, and only those with many adult learners lost their endings.

A.why: You picked the quotation that links trade to simpler grammar. That's the general observation the passage opens with. It doesn't separate adult learners from contact, and that separation is the whole of Osei's argument.

B.why: This quotation fits the background point that children learn grammar easily. It says nothing about whether adult learners or contact changes a language's grammar.

D.why: You noticed that this quotation is about languages many adults adopted. But it says those languages *gained* grammatical endings, which is the opposite of the simplification Osei describes.

stem: Which quotation from the team's report would best support Lindqvist's conclusion?
stimulus: Many vaccines require a second dose weeks after the first, and a substantial share of patients never return for it. A public health team at a regional clinic network randomly assigned patients due for a second dose to receive no message, a generic text reminder, or a text stating that a dose "has been reserved for you." The two texts were identical in timing and length. The team's lead, epidemiologist Ravi Lindqvist, concluded that the reserved-dose wording, rather than simply receiving a reminder, accounts for the improvement in return rates.
choices: Patients sent either kind of text reminder returned for their second dose at higher rates than patients who received no message.
Patients sent the reserved-dose text and those sent the generic text returned for their second dose at nearly identical rates.
Patients who missed their second dose most often said they had forgotten the date rather than doubted the vaccine's value.
Return rates were highest after the reserved-dose text; patients sent the generic text returned about as often as those sent nothing.
explanation: Before reading the choices, work out what the claim predicts. If the wording is what matters, the reserved-dose group should return more often than the generic group, and the generic group should do no better than the group sent nothing. Choice D reports exactly that pattern. It shows the gain comes from the wording rather than from getting a text at all.

A.why: You saw that the reminders helped and accepted that as support. But putting both texts together can't tell you whether the wording or the reminder itself made the difference, and that's the distinction Lindqvist draws.

B.why: You picked the quotation that compares the two texts, which is the right comparison. But it finds no difference between them, which would mean the wording didn't matter and would undercut Lindqvist's conclusion.

C.why: This quotation explains why patients miss doses, which fits the topic. It doesn't compare any of the three groups, so it can't show what caused the improvement.
